reference.source: Renal tubulopathy and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function of the basolateral chloride channel ClC-Kb, encoded by CLCNKB, which is expressed in both the thick ascending limb and the distal convoluted tubule.
This is the classic Bartter syndrome, typically presenting in infancy or early childhood rather than antenatally, though onset and severity are highly variable.
Because ClC-Kb also functions distally, the phenotype can overlap biochemically with Gitelman syndrome, sometimes with hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria rather than hypercalciuria.
Core biochemistry is hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism and normal or low blood pressure.
Hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis are less consistent than in the loop-restricted types 1 and 2.
Presentation ranges from a severe antenatal-like picture to a mild Gitelman-like phenotype.
Failure to thrive, polyuria, salt craving, muscle weakness, fatigue and constipation are common.
Large deletions of CLCNKB are a frequent molecular mechanism, so deletion analysis matters.
reference.pathophysiology: Bartter syndrome type 3 results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CLCNKB, encoding the basolateral chloride channel ClC-Kb. ClC-Kb provides the exit pathway for chloride reabsorbed at the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb, and is also expressed in the distal convoluted tubule; its loss therefore impairs sodium chloride reabsorption across both segments. This dual localisation explains the broad and variable phenotype of type 3 disease, which ranges from a severe antenatal-like presentation to a mild picture that overlaps biochemically with Gitelman syndrome, sometimes including hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria rather than the hypercalciuria typical of the loop-restricted subtypes. As with the other forms, salt wasting drives hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism and a hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis while blood pressure remains normal or low. Large gene deletions are a common molecular mechanism, and a digenic form involving both CLCNKB and CLCNKA, which share the accessory subunit barttin, underlies some overlapping presentations.
additionalDifferentials: Gitelman syndrome (SLC12A3) — the closest mimic, given the shared distal tubular involvement
Bartter syndrome type 1 (SLC12A1 / NKCC2) — antenatal, strongly hypercalciuric
Bartter syndrome type 2 (KCNJ1 / ROMK) — antenatal, with transient neonatal hyperkalaemia
Bartter syndrome types 4 and 4b (BSND / barttin; digenic CLCNKA plus CLCNKB) — with sensorineural deafness
Transient antenatal Bartter syndrome type 5 (MAGED2, X-linked)
Surreptitious diuretic misuse, laxative abuse or chronic vomiting
EAST/SeSAME syndrome (KCNJ10) — salt-losing tubulopathy with epilepsy, ataxia and deafness
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes and venous blood gas to document hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Serum magnesium, which may be low, and a urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio, which is variable and can be low, reflecting the Gitelman overlap
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, both characteristically elevated
Renal tract ultrasound, noting that nephrocalcinosis is less common than in types 1 and 2
Molecular genetic testing of CLCNKB including deletion and duplication analysis, within a tubulopathy panel, with consideration of CLCNKA for the digenic form
Audiological assessment to help exclude barttin-related type 4 disease
Spot urinary electrolytes to confirm inappropriate renal salt wasting
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia with muscle weakness, cardiac arrhythmia or rhabdomyolysis
Profound volume depletion during intercurrent illness with reduced oral intake
Progressive chronic kidney disease in longstanding disease
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is variable and mirrors the phenotypic spectrum. Many patients do well on potassium and salt replacement, with prostaglandin synthetase inhibition where needed, and maintain normal or near-normal renal function, although severe cases can be complicated by chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish it from Gitelman syndrome given the biochemical overlap, as hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria can occur
Missing large CLCNKB deletions if only sequencing is performed without deletion and duplication analysis
Overlooking barttin-related type 4 disease by not assessing hearing
Under-recognising the wide phenotypic spectrum, from severe neonatal to mild adult-diagnosed disease
